prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Follow, Though, And

outputs.L1:
Follow thy fair sun, unhappy shadow,  
Though thou be black as night,  
And she made all of light;  
Yet follow thy fair sun, unhappy shadow.

Follow her whose light thy light depriveth,  
Though here thou liv’st disgraced,  
And she in heaven is placed;  
Yet follow her whose light the world reviveth.

Follow those pure beams whose beauty burneth,  
That so have scorched thee,  
As thou still black must be,  
Till her kind beams thy black to brightness turneth.

Follow her while yet her glory shineth;  
There comes a luckless night  
That will dim all her light,  
And this the black, unhappy shade divineth.

Follow still, since so thy fates ordained:  
The sun must have his shade,  
Till both at once do fade—  
The sun still proved, the shadow still disdained.

**Poetry Out Loud Note:** In the print anthology, this poem is titled “Follow thy fair sun, unhappy shadow.” The student may give either title during the recitation.
outputs.L2:
Keep pursuing your radiant sun, sorrowful shadow. Although you are dark as midnight while she consists entirely of brightness, continue to seek her.

Go after the woman whose brilliance overwhelms your own. Though you remain on earth in disgrace while she occupies a place in heaven, follow the one whose light restores life to the world.

Pursue those flawless rays whose beauty blazes. They have burned you so deeply that you must remain dark until her gentle light transforms your darkness into radiance.

Stay with her while her splendor still glows. An unfortunate night will eventually arrive and obscure all her brightness—a fate the miserable dark shadow foresees.

Continue onward, since destiny has decreed it. The sun must be accompanied by its shadow until both disappear together: the sun forever admired and the shadow forever rejected.

**Poetry Out Loud note:** The printed anthology calls this poem **“Follow thy fair sun, unhappy shadow.”** During the recitation, the student may use either title.
outputs.L3:
The speaker urges the unhappy shadow to continue following the radiant woman, despite the darkness and disgrace that define its existence. Her beauty is portrayed as a heavenly, life-giving light: although her brilliance leaves the shadow deprived of light, it also sustains and guides it. Her pure beams have already scorched the shadow, deepening its suffering, yet the speaker holds out hope that this same radiance may ultimately transform its blackness into brightness.

The shadow must therefore remain close to the woman for as long as her glory endures. Her splendor cannot last forever, for an inevitable night will eventually descend and dim her light. Until then, fate binds the woman and the shadow together as inseparably as the sun and the darkness it casts. They will remain united until both finally fade, even though their treatment is profoundly unequal: the radiant woman is admired and honored like the sun, while the shadow that faithfully follows her is rejected and despised.
outputs.L4:
The poem develops an extended metaphor in which a dark shadow endlessly follows a radiant sun. The sun represents an admired, powerful, and seemingly unattainable beloved, while the shadow embodies a devoted figure whose existence is defined by pursuit. Because light and shadow are naturally connected, the metaphor suggests a bond that cannot easily be broken. Yet their relationship is profoundly unequal: the sun shines independently and commands attention, whereas the shadow remains secondary, obscure, and dependent on the sun’s presence.

This inequality gives the shadow’s devotion a tragic quality. Although it follows faithfully, it receives neither affection nor recognition in return. Instead, it is scorned, perhaps because its darkness contrasts so sharply with the sun’s brilliance. The shadow’s persistence therefore expresses the pain of unrequited love. It cannot reach or possess the object of its devotion, but neither can it abandon the pursuit. Its constancy may appear admirable, yet it also reveals a form of helplessness, since the shadow has no identity or direction apart from the sun.

The image of pursuit also emphasizes the power of fate. The shadow and the sun are inseparable by the laws of nature, but their closeness does not produce equality or mutual love. They remain bound together while occupying opposite symbolic positions: light and darkness, prominence and obscurity, independence and dependence. Their relationship is predetermined, leaving the shadow unable either to change its condition or to escape it.

Ultimately, however, even this apparently permanent bond must end. When the sun’s light fades, the shadow disappears with it. This shared vanishing introduces the inevitability of mortality and places both figures under the same final law. The sun may seem superior during life, but it is no less vulnerable to extinction. Thus, the poem suggests that steadfast love can survive rejection and endure suffering, yet it cannot overcome time, fate, or death. In the end, both the radiant beloved and the neglected devotee fade together, making mortality the only force that renders them equal.

counterfactuals.output:
## Follow Your Saint  
**By Thomas Campion**

Follow your saint, follow with accents sweet;  
Haste you, sad notes, fall at her flying feet.  
There, wrapt in cloud of sorrow, pity move,  
And tell the ravisher of my soul I perish for her love:  
But if she scorns my never-ceasing pain,  
Then burst with sighing in her sight and ne’er return again.

All that I sung still to her praise did tend;  
Still she was first, still she my songs did end.  
Yet she my love and music both doth fly,  
The music that her echo is and beauty’s sympathy:  
Then let my notes pursue her scornful flight;  
It shall suffice that they were breathed and died for her delight.
